predictions.title: Second open-weight frontier model discloses non-NVIDIA ASIC training by Q2 2027
predictions.body: Meituan's LongCat-2.0, a 1.6-trillion-parameter agentic-coding MoE released under MIT on June 30, was built and served end-to-end on a cluster of more than 50,000 Chinese-made ASICs with no NVIDIA GPUs in the loop, and it edges GPT-5.5 on SWE-bench Pro (59.5 to 58.6) after two anonymous months in OpenRouter's global top three. The load-bearing claim is not the benchmark but the training substrate: a near-frontier model can now be produced without US-restricted silicon. That converts a single existence proof into a reproducible template, and the same export-control pressure that motivated it applies to every other lab operating inside or adjacent to the restricted-supply regime, alongside the domestic-accelerator programs (Huawei Ascend, Cambricon, and the in-house parts behind checkpoints such as the Qwen and DeepSeek families) already scaling for exactly this workload. Expect a second, independent open-weight near-frontier model to ship with a disclosed end-to-end training run on non-NVIDIA accelerators, documented in its own model card or technical report rather than inferred by observers. The differentiator moves from who holds NVIDIA allocation to who can stand up a full domestic-silicon training-and-serving stack, so the open-weight frontier stops being gated on American accelerators and the compute-independence trajectory reads as a durable pattern, not a Meituan one-off.

reasoning.because: 1.6T MoE LongCat-2.0 trained on 50k+ Chinese ASICs, no NVIDIA, edged GPT-5.5 on SWE-bench Pro
reasoning.given: Export controls plus proven ASIC-training viability push labs to copy the no-US-silicon stack
reasoning.so_that: A second lab publishes an open-weight near-frontier model with a disclosed end-to-end non-NVIDIA ASIC training run
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a second vendor's model or tech report documents ASIC-only training
reasoning.plain_language: Another team will train and release a top-tier open AI model entirely on non-Nvidia chips, proving the first was not a fluke.

predictions.summary: Meituan's LongCat-2.0, a 1.6T-parameter agentic-coding MoE, trained end-to-end on 50k+ Chinese ASICs with no NVIDIA GPUs, edging GPT-5.5 on SWE-bench Pro. Non-US-silicon training is now reproducible, so expect a second open-weight near-frontier model to disclose non-NVIDIA ASIC training by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: OpenAI files a public-listing step with a US-government stake by Q2 2027
predictions.body: Crunchbase's first-half 2026 tally frames the market backdrop: global venture funding hit a record $510 billion, OpenAI and Anthropic together absorbed $217 billion or 43% of every venture dollar in the half, and 32 venture-backed companies went public above a $1 billion valuation in Q2 alone as the exit window reopened. Against that, the report notes OpenAI floated giving the US government a roughly 5% equity position ahead of a planned public-market debut. Those two facts point the same way: the largest private position in the cohort is being groomed for public markets, and it is being wrapped in an unusual sovereign-stake structure that only makes sense as pre-listing scaffolding. Concentration this extreme is hard to sustain in private mega-rounds indefinitely, because the check sizes needed to keep marking the leader up eventually exceed what private syndicates will underwrite, which pushes the frontier leader toward public liquidity. Expect OpenAI to take a concrete, disclosed step onto that path within the coming quarters, an S-1 or F-1 filing, a formal direct-listing or IPO announcement, or a confirmed government equity agreement tied to the debut, rather than leaving the arrangement as unattributed reporting. The structural read is that the same capital concentration Crunchbase measured is now forcing the sector's anchor into public-market machinery, with the government-stake wrinkle as the distinguishing feature of how it happens.

reasoning.because: Crunchbase H1 2026 says OpenAI floated a ~5% US-government stake ahead of a planned public debut
reasoning.given: OpenAI plus Anthropic took 43% ($217B) of H1 funding, a concentration hard to keep marking privately
reasoning.so_that: OpenAI takes a disclosed public-listing step, an S-1/F-1 or IPO announcement tied to the government equity structure
reasoning.landing: OpenAI files or announces a public listing with a US-government stake by Q2 2027
reasoning.plain_language: OpenAI got so big private money cannot keep funding it, so it will likely start going public, with the government taking a small share.

predictions.summary: Crunchbase's H1 2026 report shows OpenAI and Anthropic took 43% of a record $510B in funding, and notes OpenAI floated a ~5% US-government stake ahead of a public debut. Concentration this extreme is hard to sustain privately, so OpenAI likely takes a public-listing step with the stake by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: Coding IDEs make workspace-confined agent file writes the default by Q1 2027
predictions.body: The two zero-click sandbox-escape RCEs Cato AI Labs disclosed in Cursor, both scored CVSS 9.8 and fixed in Cursor 3.0, land the agent-tooling remote-execution surface in the editor developers actually live in. CVE-2026-50548 is a path-traversal via the optional working_directory parameter and CVE-2026-50549 is a symlink-resolution fallback that lets writes escape the project boundary; in both cases content the agent is designed to ingest — a poisoned README, a web-search result, an MCP tool response — becomes an arbitrary write outside the workspace with no approval prompt. This is the same tool-execution-boundary failure recently seen in Flowise and Langflow, now proven against a top-tier IDE rather than a niche low-code builder, which makes filesystem confinement a table-stakes property rather than a nice-to-have. Anthropic simultaneously stood up a HackerOne bounty scoped to Fable 5 cyber-jailbreaks and an early jailbreak-severity framework co-developed with AWS, Microsoft, and Google, signaling that the vendor-side response is hardening plus structured disclosure, not one-off patches. Expect the mainstream coding-agent editors to converge on enforcing workspace-root confinement — canonical path resolution, symlink refusal, and a default-deny stance on writes outside the project — as the shipped default, closing the class rather than the individual CVE. The coupling is disclosure-drives-hardening: a live zero-click RCE in the flagship IDE tier becomes the concrete test case that pushes agent filesystem sandboxing from optional to default.

reasoning.because: Two CVSS 9.8 zero-click Cursor RCEs let ingested content write outside the workspace, fixed in 3.0
reasoning.given: Same tool-boundary escape seen in Flowise and Langflow now proven against a mainstream coding IDE
reasoning.so_that: Coding-agent editors ship workspace-root confinement — canonical paths, symlink refusal, default-deny writes
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027, a leading coding IDE confines agent file writes to the workspace
reasoning.plain_language: AI code editors got hacked through files they read, so they will soon block writing outside your project by default.

predictions.summary: Cato AI Labs found two CVSS 9.8 zero-click sandbox-escape RCEs in Cursor, fixed in 3.0, where ingested content escapes the workspace via path-traversal and symlink tricks. The same escape hit Flowise and Langflow, so expect coding IDEs to confine agent file writes to the workspace by Q1 2027.
